title: <For> vs <Index>: Keyed by Item Reference vs Keyed by Array Index

progressiveExplaining.eli5: Imagine a classroom where each student has their own assigned desk. If students swap places, `<For>` moves the actual children to their new desks (good for complex objects). `<Index>` keeps the children sitting in their original chairs and just swaps their name tags and hats (good for simple lists of numbers or strings).
progressiveExplaining.junior: Solid provides two built-in list components: `<For>` and `<Index>`. `<For each={items()}>` **keys by object reference**: when items move, reorder, or are inserted, the DOM nodes move with the item, and the item passed to the callback is static while its index is a signal (`item, indexSignal`). `<Index each={items()}>` **keys by array index**: DOM nodes stay fixed at their indices, while the item passed to the callback is a signal (`itemSignal, indexInt`).
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, `<For>` and `<Index>` make different performance and DOM-reuse trade-offs. `<For>` is optimal for collections of mutable objects (e.g. lists of entities with IDs): when items are sorted or shifted, DOM elements are preserved via native `insertBefore`, and internal component state stays attached to the object. `<Index>` is optimal for lists of primitives (numbers, strings) or fixed-length tables: shifting elements avoids moving DOM nodes, instead updating the signal values bound to the static index cells.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: `<For>` uses a diffing algorithm (non-Virtual DOM, operating directly on DOM child pointers) mapping object references to rendered DOM nodes. The row callback receives `(item, index)` where `index` is `createSignal()`. `<Index>` skips DOM reconciliation entirely: it creates an array of fixed DOM slots of length `N`. The row callback receives `(itemSignal, index)`. When an element at index `i` changes value, Solid simply calls `setItemSignal(newValue)` on that slot.

codeComparison.title: When to Use <For> vs <Index>
codeComparison.summary: Use `<For>` for lists of objects where element identity matters; use `<Index>` for arrays of primitives to avoid DOM node re-allocations.

legacyOrBad.label: Wrong Choice: <For> on Primitive Arrays
legacyOrBad.snippet: <For each={numbers()}>{(num) => <input value={num} />}</For> // ❌ Re-creates DOM node on every edit

modernOrGood.label: Correct Choice: <Index> for Primitives
modernOrGood.snippet: <Index each={numbers()}>{(numSignal, index) => <input value={numSignal()} />}</Index> // ✅ NEW: Preserves DOM & focus

interviewGotchas.question: What is the key signature difference in the callback functions of `<For>` and `<Index>`?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your practical attention to detail regarding signal parameters.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: In `<For each={items}>{(item, index) => ...}</For>`, **`item` is a static value** and **`index` is a reactive accessor signal (`index()`)**. In `<Index each={items}>{(item, index) => ...}</Index>`, **`item` is a reactive accessor signal (`item()`)** and **`index` is a static number**.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Calling `item()` in a `<For>` loop will cause a `TypeError: item is not a function`. Omitting `()` on `item` in an `<Index>` loop will render the raw function representation instead of the value.

interviewGotchas.question: Why does using `<For>` on a list of primitive strings cause an `<input>` field to lose focus when the user types?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Checks understanding of object reference identity in list reconciliation.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Primitives in JavaScript (strings, numbers) are compared by value. When the user types a new character, the string value changes (e.g. `'a'` -> `'ab'`). Because `<For>` tracks identity by reference/value, it considers `'a'` destroyed and `'ab'` a completely new item, destroying the old DOM `<input>` element and creating a new one, which immediately drops keyboard focus.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Always use `<Index>` when mapping arrays of primitive strings/numbers or when mutating by index.
